content: Seborrhoeic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that occurs globally and commonly affects areas such as the scalp, face, and body folds. Treatment options include antifungal agents, corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, keratolytic agents, and phototherapy. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of topical antifungal treatments for seborrhoeic dermatitis in adolescents and adults, with a secondary focus on their efficacy in individuals with HIV/AIDS. To gather evidence, databases such as the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS were searched up to December 2014. Additional sources included trial registries and bibliographies of published studies. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed topical antifungals for seborrhoeic dermatitis, with primary outcomes being complete symptom clearance and improved quality of life. A total of 51 studies involving 9,052 participants were included. Most trials (45) evaluated outcomes within five weeks of treatment initiation, while six studies assessed longer-term outcomes. Twenty-four trials had potential conflicts of interest, such as pharmaceutical company funding. The studies included 12 trials on ketoconazole (3,253 participants), 11 on ciclopirox (3,029 participants), two on lithium (141 participants), two on bifonazole (136 participants), and one on clotrimazole (126 participants). These trials compared the antifungal agents to placebo, vehicle, steroids, or other antifungals. Ketoconazole Topical ketoconazole 2% reduced the risk of failed rash clearance by 31% compared to placebo at four weeks of follow-up (risk ratio [RR] 0.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.59 to 0.81, eight studies, low-quality evidence). However, the effect on side effects was uncertain due to very low-quality evidence (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.64, six studies), and there was significant heterogeneity between studies (I² = 74%). In placebo groups, the median proportion of participants without rash clearance was 69%. Ketoconazole showed a similar remission rate to steroids (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.44, six studies, low-quality evidence), but side effects were 44% less frequent in the ketoconazole group compared to the steroid group (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.96, eight studies, moderate-quality evidence). Ketoconazole also had a comparable remission failure rate to ciclopirox (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.26, three studies, low-quality evidence). Most comparisons between ketoconazole and other antifungals were based on single studies, which generally showed similar treatment effects. Ciclopirox Ciclopirox 1% was associated with a lower failed remission rate compared to placebo at four weeks of follow-up (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.94, eight studies, moderate-quality evidence). Side effect rates were similar between ciclopirox and placebo (RR 0.9, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.11, four studies, moderate-quality evidence). Other Antifungals Clotrimazole and miconazole demonstrated similar short-term efficacy to steroids in single studies. However, treatment effects on individual symptoms were inconsistent, likely due to challenges in measuring these outcomes. There was insufficient evidence to determine whether the dose or mode of delivery influenced treatment outcomes. Only one study reported on treatment compliance, and no studies assessed quality of life. One study evaluated the maximum rash-free period but provided insufficient data for analysis. A small study in HIV-positive patients compared lithium to placebo for seborrhoeic dermatitis of the face, but no significant differences in treatment outcomes were observed. Conclusions Ketoconazole and ciclopirox were more effective than placebo for seborrhoeic dermatitis, but there is limited evidence to suggest that either is superior to other antifungal agents within the same class. Few studies assessed symptom clearance beyond four weeks. Ketoconazole showed similar efficacy to steroids but with fewer side effects. The impact of antifungal treatments on overall quality of life remains unknown. Future research should focus on better outcome measures, higher-quality studies, and improved reporting to strengthen the evidence base for antifungal treatments for seborrhoeic dermatitis.
